questions.question: To find a maximum zero-cost matching in an $n\times n$ reduced cost matrix, a network with source $S$, one vertex per row, one per column and sink $T$ is built. Which edges and capacities does it use?
options: $S$ to every row, row to every column, every column to $T$; capacity equal to the entry
$S$ to every row, row to column at each zero entry, every column to $T$; all capacity 1
$S$ to every column, column to row at zero entries, every row to $T$; all capacity $n$
$S$ to every row, row to column at nonzero entries, every column to $T$; all capacity 1

questions.question: For an $n\times n$ reduced cost matrix, the matching network has source $S$, row and column vertices and sink $T$, with capacity-1 edges $S$-to-row, row-to-column at zero entries, and column-to-$T$. Why do the source-to-row and column-to-sink edges have capacity 1?
options: So that only entries with cost exactly zero can carry any flow
So that the augmenting path algorithm needs fewer augmentations
So that the flow on every middle edge is automatically a whole number
So that no row and no column is used in more than one selected pair

questions.question: For an $n\times n$ reduced cost matrix, the matching network has source $S$, row and column vertices and sink $T$, with capacity-1 edges $S$-to-row, row-to-column at zero entries, and column-to-$T$. An integral maximum flow is computed. What does its value equal?
options: The number of rows that contain at least one zero entry
The total number of zero entries in the reduced cost matrix
The largest number of zeros with no two in one row or column
The smallest total cost of any complete assignment of the rows

questions.question: For an $n\times n$ reduced cost matrix, the matching network has source $S$, row and column vertices and sink $T$, with capacity-1 edges $S$-to-row, row-to-column at zero entries, and column-to-$T$. After an integral maximum flow is found, where are the selected row-column pairs read off?
options: From the row-to-column edges that carry flow 1
From the source-to-row edges that carry flow 1
From all row-to-column edges in the network
From the column-to-sink edges that carry flow 0

questions.question: In the unit-capacity flow network for zero-cost matching of an $n\times n$ reduced cost matrix (source to rows, rows to columns, columns to sink), why are row-to-column edges placed only at zero entries?
options: A unit through an edge should mean a pair that costs nothing
Zero entries are the cheapest, so they shorten the flow paths
Nonzero entries would make the flow value exceed $n$
Zero entries are the only ones the flow can saturate

questions.question: A reduced cost matrix is $\begin{pmatrix}0&3&0\\2&0&4\\0&5&1\end{pmatrix}$. In the zero-cost matching network (source, row vertices, column vertices, sink, unit capacities), which row-to-column edges are created?

A $4\times4$ reduced cost matrix has 6 zero entries. The zero-cost matching network has a source, a sink, one vertex per row and per column, source-to-row edges, row-to-column edges at zeros and column-to-sink edges. How many vertices and edges does it have?
options: 10 vertices and 24 edges
10 vertices and 14 edges
8 vertices and 6 edges
6 vertices and 14 edges

questions.question: In the zero-cost matching network of a $3\times3$ reduced cost matrix, an integral maximum flow sends 1 unit on $S\to r_1$, $S\to r_2$, $r_1\to c_2$, $r_2\to c_1$, $c_1\to T$, $c_2\to T$ and 0 on all other edges, including $r_3\to c_1$. Which zero-cost pairs are selected?
options: Rows 1 and 2, with their columns still open
Pairs $(1,1)$ and $(2,2)$, matching equal numbers
Row 1 with column 2, row 2 and row 3 with column 1
Row 1 with column 2 and row 2 with column 1

questions.question: A $3\times3$ reduced cost matrix has zeros exactly at positions $(1,2)$, $(2,1)$, $(2,2)$, $(2,3)$ and $(3,2)$. What is the value of an integral maximum flow in its zero-cost matching network?

For an $n\times n$ reduced cost matrix, the matching network has source $S$, row and column vertices and sink $T$, with capacity-1 edges $S$-to-row, row-to-column at zero entries, and column-to-$T$. For $n=4$, an integral maximum flow has value 3. What does this tell about assigning rows to columns at zero cost?
options: A complete zero-cost assignment exists, with one zero spare
At most 3 rows get zero-cost columns; one row is left out
The matrix contains exactly 3 zero entries in total
Three of the four rows contain no zero entry at all

questions.question: For an $n\times n$ reduced cost matrix, the matching network has source $S$, row and column vertices and sink $T$, with capacity-1 edges $S$-to-row, row-to-column at zero entries, and column-to-$T$. Why does the augmenting path algorithm, started from zero flow, give a flow in which every edge carries 0 or 1?
options: Each capacity is 1, so each augmentation moves 1 unit and flows stay whole
The algorithm rounds each flow to the nearest whole number at the very end
Any maximum flow of this network is integral, whatever method finds it
The edges at zero entries have capacity 0.5, which halves each augmentation

questions.question: For an $n\times n$ reduced cost matrix, the matching network has source $S$, row and column vertices and sink $T$, with capacity-1 edges $S$-to-row, row-to-column at zero entries, and column-to-$T$. During the augmenting path algorithm an augmenting path uses the backward residual direction of a row-to-column edge $r_1\to c_1$ that currently carries flow 1. What does this step do to the matching?
options: It changes the reduced cost of entry $(1,1)$ to a nonzero value
It adds a second column to row 1, next to the column 1 it keeps
It cancels pair row 1-column 1; row 1 is re-matched elsewhere
It is not allowed, since flow may only follow the edge directions

questions.question: For an $n\times n$ reduced cost matrix, the matching network has source $S$, row and column vertices and sink $T$, with capacity-1 edges $S$-to-row, row-to-column at zero entries, and column-to-$T$. A matching of zero entries is built row by row, and no further zero pair can be added without removing one. Must its size equal the maximum flow value?
options: Yes, provided that it was built starting from the first row
Yes, since no zero pair can be added to it any more
No, an augmenting path may still exist to re-match rows
No, because the maximum flow counts all zero entries

questions.question: A $3\times3$ reduced cost matrix has zeros at $(1,1)$, $(1,2)$, $(2,1)$, $(3,2)$ and $(3,3)$. In its unit-capacity matching network the current flow uses $r_1\to c_1$ and $r_3\to c_3$. Which is an augmenting path in the residual network?
options: $S\to r_2\to c_1\to r_1\to c_2\to T$
$S\to r_2\to c_1\to r_3\to c_2\to T$
$S\to r_2\to c_2\to r_3\to c_3\to T$
$S\to r_1\to c_2\to r_3\to c_3\to T$

questions.question: A $2\times2$ reduced cost matrix has all four entries 0. An LP solver returns a maximum flow of value 2 in the unit-capacity matching network with 0.5 units on each of the four row-to-column edges. What should be done to read off the zero-cost pairs?
options: Select all four pairs, since every middle edge carries positive flow
Find an integral maximum flow, e.g. by augmenting, and read its 1s
Round every 0.5 up to 1, which gives the selected pairs at once
Conclude that only 1 pair can be matched, as $2\cdot0.5=1$

questions.question: A $4\times4$ reduced cost matrix has zeros at $(1,1)$, $(1,2)$, $(2,1)$, $(2,3)$, $(3,3)$, $(4,3)$ and $(4,4)$. Which set of pairs is a maximum zero-cost matching, as an integral maximum flow would give?

For an $n\times n$ reduced cost matrix, the matching network has source $S$, row and column vertices and sink $T$, with capacity-1 edges $S$-to-row, row-to-column at zero entries, and column-to-$T$. A student changes the capacities of the row-to-column edges from 1 to a very large number, keeping all source and sink edges at capacity 1. How does the maximum flow value change?
options: It can grow, since one zero entry may now carry several units
It is unchanged, as rows and columns still pass one unit at most
It can grow, since a row may now send flow to several columns
It drops to 0, since the middle edges are no longer unit-capacity edges

questions.question: For an $n\times n$ reduced cost matrix, the matching network has source $S$, row and column vertices and sink $T$, with capacity-1 edges $S$-to-row, row-to-column at zero entries, and column-to-$T$. The augmenting path algorithm stops with a flow of value $k$ because the residual network has no $S$-$T$ path. Why can no zero-cost matching have more than $k$ pairs?
options: It would be a larger flow, yet having no augmenting path means the flow is maximum
The algorithm has tried every set of zero pairs, so a larger one would have been found
The number of zero entries in the matrix equals $k$ when the algorithm stops
A larger matching would need the Hungarian adjustment, which this network omits

questions.question: A $4\times4$ reduced cost matrix has zeros at $(1,1)$, $(2,1)$, $(3,2)$, $(3,3)$ and $(4,4)$, so every row and every column contains a zero. What is the value of an integral maximum flow in its zero-cost matching network?

A $3\times3$ reduced cost matrix has zeros at $(1,1)$, $(1,2)$, $(1,3)$, $(2,1)$ and $(3,1)$. In its matching network a student gives every source-to-row edge capacity 3, keeping all other capacities 1. What maximum flow value results?
options: 1, since only row 1 gains any extra capacity
2, the same value as with unit capacities
5, one unit through each of the five zeros
3, which overstates the true maximum of 2
